passage:
Diary, Saturday
I got my hair cut short like the captain of our women's team. Everyone at the nets says I look like a boy. I don't care. I'm the only girl there anyway. I practised her stance for one hour in the garage: bat up high, chin down, eyes still. I even did her little double tap of the bat before each ball. At the nets I hit three fours in a row!! I felt STRONG.
But then I copied the other thing she does, pointing the bat at the bowler after a four. Minakshi was bowling and she stopped smiling. Coach said, "Hit hard. No pointing." I felt silly.
Tomorrow: same stance, no pointing. The captain always shakes hands after matches too. I'll copy that.
Sharmila

qa.q: How many fours did Sharmila hit in a row at the nets?
qa.a: Three fours in a row.

qa.q: Why did Sharmila feel 'STRONG' when she used the captain's stance?
qa.a: Copying her hero made her feel some of the captain's power and confidence, and hitting fours seemed to prove it. 😊

qa.q: What choice did Sharmila make about which habits to copy, and why is it wise?
qa.a: Keeping the stance and the handshakes but dropping the pointing, because the handshake shows respect while the pointing only upset Minakshi.

qa.q: How might Minakshi have felt when Sharmila pointed the bat at her?
qa.a: Minakshi probably felt mocked or shown up, which is why she stopped smiling.

grounding: A girl copies her cricket hero's haircut, stance and gestures, feels stronger, and learns the swagger doesn't come with the skill.

passage:
Nine-year-old Indu, in her village outside Karnal, had pinned up a newspaper photo of the district's gold-medal sprinter, a young woman who had grown up three villages away. Indu now tied her hair in the same high knot, wore a sweatband on one wrist, and started every morning with the warm-up she had seen on the TV at the tea stall. She even walked like her, shoulders back. "Early to bed, early to track," she told her little sister Payal, in the sprinter's firm voice.
But when Payal beat her in a race to the well, Indu snapped, "Champions don't lose to babies," and stalked off. Payal's lip wobbled. That evening Indu came back with a guava. "Champions also say sorry," she mumbled.

qa.q: What did Indu wear on one wrist?
qa.a: A sweatband.

qa.q: Why did Indu snap 'Champions don't lose to babies' at Payal?
qa.a: Losing hurt her new champion image, and she borrowed a proud, swaggering attitude to cover the embarrassment.

qa.q: What turning point shows Indu choosing the better part of her hero?
qa.a: Coming back with a guava and saying 'Champions also say sorry', which keeps the discipline and drops the swagger.

qa.q: How might Payal feel about her sister's new champion act?
qa.a: Admiring at first, then hurt when the swagger turned on her; the apology probably made her feel close again.

grounding: A village girl copies a local sprinting champion's style and voice, feels stronger, and briefly borrows the swagger too.

passage:
At his Saturday cricket club in south London, eleven-year-old Jin had started copying his favourite batter from the television: the same blond streak in his fringe (his mum had allowed one), the same wide stance, the same slow walk to the crease. With the stance, his drives actually got better. He felt taller walking out. Chidi, who opened the batting with him, said, "You look like a proper pro."
But Jin also started copying the batter's hard stare at bowlers and the muttering at umpires. When the club umpire gave him out leg before wicket, Jin threw his bat down. Coach took him aside. "Your hero hits beautifully. Copy that. And copy how he apologises afterwards, too." Jin went red and picked up his bat.

qa.q: What did Jin's mum allow him to dye?
qa.a: One blond streak in his fringe.

qa.q: Why did Jin feel taller walking out to bat?
qa.a: Copying his hero's stance and walk made him feel some of the batter's strength and confidence, and his better drives seemed to prove it.

qa.q: What choice did Coach help Jin see?
qa.a: To keep copying the good batting and the apologies, but drop the stare and the bat-throwing swagger.

qa.q: How might the club umpire have felt when Jin threw his bat?
qa.a: Disrespected and uncomfortable, since a young player was treating a fair decision as an insult.

grounding: A boy in London copies a cricket hero's look and stance, feels stronger, and also picks up the hero's swagger.

passage:
At the district cricket academy, Shalini, eleven, had become someone else. Her favourite fast bowler wore a tight side braid, so Shalini did too. She copied the long run-up, the hard stare down the pitch, the knee-slide after a wicket. She arrived at six to do the bowler's shadow drills from a video, and her line had never been better.
On Thursday she bowled a small Class 3 boy, then walked up to him and said, "Go home, baby," just like the clip. A few kids laughed. The boy's lip shook.
Coach Lalremsiami called Shalini over. "Your run-up is superb. Coming at six is exactly what your hero does. The 'go home, baby' part, though? Would she say that to a little kid?"
Shalini looked at her shoes. "Maybe not to a little kid."

qa.q: What did Shalini say to the Class 3 boy she bowled?
qa.a: "Go home, baby."

qa.q: Why might copying the fast bowler's stare and celebration feel good to Shalini?
qa.a: Copying her hero makes Shalini feel powerful and confident, and that confidence pushes her to train harder too.

qa.q: What choice by Coach Lalremsiami sorted the good from the bad?
qa.a: The coach praised the run-up and the early training but questioned the sledge, helping Shalini keep the hero's values and drop the swagger.

qa.q: What was that moment like for the Class 3 boy?
qa.a: Already out, he was mocked by an older player in front of others, so he likely felt small and embarrassed, fighting tears.

grounding: Shows a child who copies a fast bowler's style and training, gaining strength and discipline but also picking up swagger that a coach helps separate.

passage:
I'm Harsha, and I run the Sunday cricket in our colony lane. For a month Gargi, nine, has been turning into her favourite batter. Same short haircut, same tap-tap of the bat on the ground, same slow twirl after every shot. She even practises forward defence a hundred times against our wall before school, because she read that her hero does.
Her batting really has got better. But last Sunday, when Sunny gave her out lbw, she threw her head back, rolled her eyes like on TV, and walked off without the handshake. Nobody knew what to say.
I don't know what she was thinking. Maybe she felt like a star. Later I saw her sitting on the steps, bat across her knees, watching the others play.

qa.q: How many times does Gargi practise forward defence before school?
qa.a: A hundred times, against the wall.

qa.q: What might Gargi have felt as she rolled her eyes and walked off?
qa.a: She may have felt like a real star copying her hero, but the swagger also covered disappointment at getting out; sitting alone later suggests it didn't feel good.

qa.q: How could Harsha help Gargi keep the good parts of copying her hero?
qa.a: Harsha could praise the practice and the improved batting, then remind Gargi that the handshake is part of the game, even for stars.

qa.q: How might Sunny have felt when Gargi rolled her eyes at the lbw decision?
qa.a: Sunny was only doing the umpire's job, so the eye-roll probably felt unfair and awkward, and might make Sunny unsure about umpiring again.

grounding: Illustrates, through an older neighbour's eyes, a child who adopts a batter's look and practice habits, improving her game but also importing an eye-rolling swagger.

passage:
Coach's note, under-twelve girls' cricket, Pune.
Since the national series on TV, Shalini, eleven, has turned herself into a copy of the star opener Kaveri Bose. The red headband. The high backlift. The way she taps her bat twice. Her batting has actually improved; she stands taller, braver. But she's also copied the glare. Today, after hitting a four, she stared down Sabina, the bowler, and said, "Is that all you've got?" Sabina's face fell. What I did next: I sat Shalini down and told her I love the headband and the backlift. Then I asked, "What does Kaveri do after a match?" She thought. "She shakes hands with everyone." "So take that from her too." Shalini nodded. At the end of practice, she shook Sabina's hand.

qa.q: Who is Shalini copying?
qa.a: The star opener Kaveri Bose.

qa.q: Why does Shalini stand taller when she copies Kaveri Bose?
qa.a: Copying her hero makes Shalini feel braver and stronger, as if she has some of Kaveri's power.

qa.q: What did the coach do well?
qa.a: The coach praised what was good, then pointed Shalini to her hero's sportsmanship, helping her drop the swagger without shaming her.

qa.q: How might Sabina have felt when Shalini glared at her?
qa.a: Sabina probably felt hurt and small, taunted after being hit for four.

grounding: Shows a child copying a cricketer's stance and attitude, feeling some of the hero's strength, while also importing swagger.

passage:
Dear diary, Lakshmi here.

I have decided I am going to be exactly like Veer Shetty, the kabaddi raider on TV. I cut my fringe short like his. I practise his crouch in the corridor. And I say, "Come on then!" before every raid, like he does, with my chin up.

Today in PE, I did the crouch and the chin and I actually got two points! I felt like Veer. Like nothing could stop me.

But then when I was out, I kicked the mat like he did in the final. Coach said, "Lakshmi, we don't kick the mat here." Madhuri, my sister, said it looked silly.

I don't think it looked silly. He's the best.

Okay, maybe the mat part was a bit much. But the crouch stays.

qa.q: How many points did Lakshmi get in PE?
qa.a: Two points.

qa.q: How did Lakshmi feel doing the crouch and chin like Veer Shetty?
qa.a: Lakshmi felt powerful and proud, as if some of the hero's strength came from copying him.

qa.q: What could Lakshmi keep from Veer Shetty, and what could she drop?
qa.a: Lakshmi could keep the crouch and the confidence, which help her play, and drop the mat-kicking, which is swagger that doesn't fit the team.

qa.q: How might Madhuri see Lakshmi's new style?
qa.a: Madhuri finds parts of it silly, though Madhuri may also notice how proud and excited Lakshmi is.

grounding: Shows a child copying a sports hero's stance, hairstyle and attitude, feeling stronger but also picking up some swagger.

passage: In the village near Muzaffarpur, everyone talked about Bhola Yadav, the district cricketer who had played for the state. Nikita, nine, wanted to be him. She turned her collar up like Bhola bhaiya. She walked with her shoulders back, spinning the tennis ball on one finger. On the dusty ground behind the school, she batted his way, feet wide, and hit the ball over the neem tree. The boys whistled. Nikita felt ten feet tall. Then, when little Pinku dropped a catch, she snapped, "Useless! Go home!" the way Bhola bhaiya shouted at his fielders. Pinku's lip trembled. Her big brother Siddharth, fielding at the back, walked over. "Bhola bhaiya shouts, but that's the bit nobody likes," he said quietly. "Keep the batting." Nikita looked at Pinku. "Sorry. Try again," she said, and threw him the ball.

qa.q: Where did Nikita hit the ball?
qa.a: Over the neem tree.

qa.q: Why did Nikita feel ten feet tall?
qa.a: Copying Bhola Yadav's style made her feel strong and proud, as if she had some of his power.

qa.q: How did Siddharth help Nikita without shaming her?
qa.a: He quietly pointed out which part of the hero to keep and which to drop, without mocking her.

qa.q: How might Pinku have felt when Nikita called him useless?
qa.a: Pinku probably felt hurt and ashamed, being shouted at like a grown-up fielder.

grounding: Shows a child copying a local cricketer's stance and attitude, gaining confidence but also borrowing his harshness.

passage:
In Bergen, Astrid had watched the national team captain's goal replay forty times. By Monday she had the same high ponytail with a red band, the same way of tapping her boots together before a free kick, the same serious squint.

At training she felt taller. She stayed after to practise corners, as the captain said in interviews: "Nobody gets lucky without practice."

But she also copied the captain's shrug when the coach corrected her, and on Wednesday, when her little brother Liam missed a pass, she rolled her eyes and said, "Some of us are professionals." Liam's face crumpled.

That night she watched the replay again. After the goal, the captain went straight to help up a defender who had fallen. Astrid hadn't noticed that before.

qa.q: How many times had Astrid watched the goal replay?
qa.a: Astrid had watched it forty times.

qa.q: How does copying the captain make Astrid feel at training?
qa.a: Astrid feels taller and more confident, as if a little of the captain's strength is hers.

qa.q: What could Astrid copy next from the captain?
qa.a: Astrid could copy the captain helping up the fallen defender, and apologise to Liam for the professionals remark.

qa.q: What was it like for Liam on Wednesday?
qa.a: Liam felt hurt and small when his sister rolled her eyes and mocked his missed pass.

grounding: Shows a girl who copies a football captain's look and habits, gaining practice values but also picking up swagger.

passage:
At the school cricket nets in Indore, Payal had stopped being Payal. She was "the opener". She wore her collar up like the women's opener on TV, tapped her bat three times at the crease, and walked to the pitch with the same slow swagger.

Her batting really had improved. She watched the ball longer, just as the opener said in interviews, and practised straight drives until dark.

But on Thursday, when Coach Tarun asked her to field at short leg, she said, "Openers don't field there, sir." Two younger girls giggled nervously.

Coach Tarun didn't shout. "Your opener dives at short leg every match. Didn't you see?" Payal went red. She jogged to short leg and crouched, collar still up.

qa.q: How many times did Payal tap her bat at the crease?
qa.a: Payal tapped her bat three times.

qa.q: Why might Payal walk with the opener's swagger?
qa.a: Payal admires the opener and feels stronger and more confident when she moves like her hero.

qa.q: How did Coach Tarun turn the admiration toward good values?
qa.a: He pointed out that the opener herself fields at short leg, using Payal's hero to teach teamwork instead of scolding.

qa.q: How might the two younger girls see Payal's refusal?
qa.a: They seemed nervous, perhaps unsure whether to admire her or feel uneasy about her talking back to the coach.

grounding: Shows a girl who copies a cricketer's stance and swagger, improving her batting but also borrowing attitude.

Before, the Saturday of the final: Ujjwal watched the star batsman's hundred on TV and practised the celebration in the mirror: bat raised, finger to lips, a slow look round the stands.

During, Tuesday: Ujjwal came to school with his hair spiked like the star's. In the colony match he scored twelve, then did the full finger-to-lips celebration right in front of the bowler, Akash, who was only eight. Akash threw the ball down and went home. Ujjwal felt amazing for about five minutes.

After, Sunday: Ujjwal saw a clip of the same star after a match, shaking every opponent's hand and signing a little boy's cap. He thought about Akash's face. In the next match he scored nine, raised his bat, and then went to shake Akash's hand.

passage: Manoj, you've cut your hair like that fast bowler on TV, haven't you? When I was ten, your Swati nani did the same. There was a famous batswoman then, and I copied everything: her short hair, the way she tapped her bat twice, even her walk. That summer I felt brave, as if some of her strength had got into me. I practised every evening because she did. But I also copied her glare at bowlers, and one day I shouted at a younger girl who dropped a catch, the way I'd seen my hero do. My coach took me aside: "Copy her practice, Swati. Not her temper." I cried, but I remembered it. You can keep the haircut, beta. Just choose what else you borrow.

qa.q: How many times did the batswoman tap her bat?
qa.a: Twice.

qa.q: How did young Swati feel copying her hero?
qa.a: Brave and strong, as if some of the hero's strength had got into her.

qa.q: What was the turning point in the story?
qa.a: Her coach telling her to copy the hero's practice, not her temper, after she shouted at a younger girl.

qa.q: How might the younger girl who dropped the catch have felt?
qa.a: Hurt and scared, shouted at by an older player for one mistake.

passage: All through the monsoon, the colony cricket matches kept getting rained off, but Yogesh practised his hero's stance in the corridor anyway: bat high, collar up, chin raised. He had even asked the barber for the same spiky hair as the famous opener on TV. When he batted, he felt taller. At the one match that finally happened, he hit two fours and then stared the bowler down, just like on TV, and said, "Is that all you've got?" He mumbled sorry to the bowler.

qa.q: How many fours did Yogesh hit?
qa.a: Two.

qa.q: How did Yogesh feel batting in his hero's style?
qa.a: Taller and more confident, as if he shared some of the hero's strength.

passage: In the Christmas holidays, Deepika watched every match of the women's cricket tournament on TV in their Bengaluru flat. By New Year she had the same ponytail as her favourite captain, the same wristband, and the same way of pointing at the sky after a good shot. At the park she practised the captain's calm walk out to bat. "You even talk like her now," her friend Noor laughed. It was true. When Deepika missed a catch, she didn't cry like before; she clapped once and said, "Next ball," just like her hero. But when she hit a six, she also shouted "Too easy!" at Noor, who was bowling. Noor frowned. Deepika paused, then grinned sheepishly. "Okay, she doesn't say that part."

qa.q: What did Deepika do after a good shot?
qa.a: Pointed at the sky.

qa.q: How did Deepika feel now when she missed a catch?
qa.a: Steadier and calmer; instead of crying, she clapped once, feeling some of her hero's composure.

qa.q: What did Deepika's admiration teach her, and what went too far?
qa.a: Calm resilience, "Next ball"; the "Too easy!" taunt went too far, and she noticed it herself.

qa.q: How did Noor react to "Too easy!"?
qa.a: Noor frowned, a bit hurt or annoyed as the bowler.

grounding: A girl copies her cricket hero's style and calm, but catches herself importing a boastful taunt.

passage:
"Sachin, why are you standing like that?" Deepak asked, leaning on the bat at the colony ground. It was the last week of the summer holidays and dust was everywhere.
"This is how the Captain stands. Bat up, collar up." Sachin flicked his hair, freshly cut into a spike like the poster on his wall.
"Okay, fine. But why did you just tell Vinay he bowls like a grandmother?"
"The Captain says that to bowlers. It's mind games."
"Vinay's nine and it's his first match, yaar."
Sachin paused, still holding the pose. "The Captain also practises four hours every day."
"Copy that part, then. And say sorry to Vinay."

qa.a: Freshly cut into a spike like the poster on his wall.

qa.q: Why does Sachin stand with his bat up and collar up?
qa.a: He admires the Captain, and copying the stance makes him feel a little of the hero's strength and confidence.

qa.q: What advice does Deepak give, and why is it good?
qa.a: Copy the Captain's four hours of practice, not the teasing, and say sorry to Vinay 👍; keep the useful value and drop the swagger.

qa.q: How might Vinay feel about Sachin's "mind games"?
qa.a: Vinay, playing his first match, probably felt hurt and nervous at being told he bowls like a grandmother.
